title: The Value of a Disposition: An Ontological Argument for Quantifying Dispositions
abstract: The distinction between categorical and dispositional properties has found its way into ontological engineering as a distinction between types of dependent entities: qualities and dispositions. They are distinguished, of course, by their corresponding natures, which is reflected in the association of dispositions with occurrent types that represent their possible manifestations, while qualities have no such association. Another distinction is that qualities are commonly associated to values (called qualia), while dispositions are not. The association with values, however, has nothing to do with the categorical nature of qualities, but rather with the necessity of quantifying such properties. We see no reason why the quantification of properties should be restricted to qualities. In fact, many common dispositions are associated with values, particularly in scientific contexts. Throughout this paper, we argue for the conception of values of dispositions as individuals in ontological models. Those values ground comparative relations between dispositions and their change over time, and may play a prominent role in ensuring the parsimony and expressivity of dispositional models, as well as in integrating ontological and mathematical frameworks. We also dive briefly into the nature of dispositional value, discussing distinct approaches for its definition.

title: Weakly Supervised Learning of Oral Cavity Images for Separating Precancer from Cancer
abstract: Early detection is crucial for reducing the morbidity and mortality associated with oral cancer. Visual examination of the oral cavity is the first step in screening for lesions that are cancer or precancer (i.e., the direct precursor to cancer). In contrast to existing work that uses image or lesion labels, we explore a weakly supervised method to address the situation where only patient-level labels are available. Specifically, we use multiple-instance learning (MIL) to classify patients with oral precancer versus cancer. Our approach involves three steps: image filtering, mouth detection, and patient-level classification. The method performs well on filtering and mouth detection and shows promising results in distinguishing precancer from cancer on an independent test set, demonstrating its potential as a proof-of-concept (PoC). We also discuss current limitations and future directions.

title: AMRA: a lightweight adapter endowing LLMS with the capability to perform robust multimodal sentiment analysis
abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) aims to integrate heterogeneous information from text, visual, and acoustic modalities to understand human intent. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable representation capabilities, applying them to multimodal tasks often incurs high computational costs and suffers from modality conflict. To address this, we propose the Adaptive Multi-modal Routing Adapter (AMRA), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for LLMs. By incorporating a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism into the adapter architecture, AMRA enables the frozen LLM to dynamically select the most relevant experts for processing multi-modal inputs. This routing mechanism not only resolves modality ambiguity but also significantly reduces trainable parameters. Extensive experiments on the large-scale benchmark dataset CMU-MOSEI demonstrate that AMRA achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines, proving its effectiveness in empowering LLMs for multimodal tasks.

title: LLM-guided counterfactual reasoning for explainable clinical risk prediction
abstract: Deep learning models have demonstrated promising performance in clinical natural language processing (NLP), yet their black-box nature limits clinical interpretability and trustworthiness. Although post-hoc explainability methods such as attention visualization, SHAP, and LIME identify influential features, they provide limited insight into how clinically meaningful modifications to a patient’s narrative would alter the model prediction. This paper proposes a structured large language model (LLM)-guided counterfactual explanation framework for interpreting black-box ClinicalBERT models predicting opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD). Unlike conventional single-prompt prompting strategies, the proposed methodology decomposes counterfactual generation into three sequential reasoning stages: (i) latent clinical concept identification, (ii) localization of the corresponding textual evidence, and (iii) controlled generation of minimally modified counterfactual clinical narratives. This structured prompting strategy improves the transparency and controllability of the explanation process while preserving the semantic coherence and clinical plausibility of the generated narratives. The proposed framework was evaluated using three state-of-the-art open-source LLMs, namely DeepSeek-R1 (14B), Qwen2.5-Coder (32B), and Llama-3.1 (8B)-Instruct, for explaining the predictions of a fine-tuned ClinicalBERT OIRD classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently generates clinically meaningful counterfactual explanations capable of altering model predictions through minimal and targeted textual modifications. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-Coder (32B) achieved the highest counterfactual generation success rate, while DeepSeek-R1 (14B) produced explanations with superior semantic preservation and clinical coherence. The comparative analysis further demonstrates that the proposed framework is model-agnostic and can be readily integrated with different LLMs without modifying the underlying prediction model. These findings suggest that the proposed structured prompting framework provides a practical and generalizable approach for improving explainability and transparency in clinical NLP systems and has the potential to support trustworthy AI-assisted clinical decision making.

title: Rare earth element geochemical exploration: Anomalies in stream sediments across climatic and geological regimes in the southern Andes, Chile
abstract: Rare earth element (REE) exploration in Chile remains uneven despite strong climatic, geomorphic, and lithological contrasts that are favorable for multiple REE source models. This study compiles 6926 fine-fraction (<180 µm) stream-sediment samples from the Chilean national geochemical survey and evaluates them across six geo-climatic clusters ranging from hyper-arid to cold-temperate environments. Using major- and trace-element geochemistry, weathering indices, spatial hot-spot analysis, robust principal component analysis, and REE lambda coefficients, we assess how REE signatures vary across the country and what they imply for exploration targeting. The results reveal systematic inter-cluster differences not only in REE abundances, but also in REE-pattern geometry, spatial coherence, and multivariate structure. Cluster 3 displays the most diagnostic weathering-related REE signature, with coherent positive Ce anomalies and strong evidence of chemical redistribution, making it the clearest analogue for regolith-hosted REE prospectivity. However, these signatures also suggest that stream-sediment anomalies in such environments may reflect active REE mobilization rather than in situ accumulation. Cluster 4 preserves part of this signal in a more diffuse form, whereas the northern clusters (C1–C2b) are more consistent with mixed source models involving IOA/IOCG-related REE carriers and detrital heavy-mineral concentration. Cluster 5 defines a distinct HREE-permissive field compatible with alkaline to locally peralkaline source environments. Overall, the results show that stream-sediment geochemistry, when integrated with spatial and multivariate approaches, can effectively distinguish contrasting REE source models at reconnaissance scale. More importantly, they show that REE anomalies are process-dependent and must be interpreted in terms of weathering, transport, and lithological controls.

title: Amortized Opacity Marginalization Improves C/O Interval Calibration for Brown-Dwarf Retrievals
abstract: Molecular line lists disagree at a level that measurably shifts retrieved C/O, so retrievals conditioned on a single list omit a dominant systematic from their error bars. Classical marginalization re-runs a full retrieval under K opacity realizations per object. We move that cost into simulation: while generating the training set we randomize opacities (smooth multiplicative Fourier fields in logν plus a discrete line-list mixture, under a deliberately broad prior informed by measured inter-list differences), so a neural posterior estimator learns an already-marginalized posterior. Conceptually, this is the amortized analogue of repeating a conventional retrieval under many plausible opacity realizations and averaging the resulting posteriors. On perturbed held-out spectra (n=2048) a standard NPE covers nominal 90% C/O intervals 43.3% of the time against 82.4% for a compute-matched marginalized network; three-seed control ensembles reach 93.2% on clean data but 61.4% under perturbation, against 89.4% marginalized, isolating the deficit as opacity-induced (TARP joint expected-coverage deviation 0.005 against 0.035). An axis ablation traces the gain to the continuous field (45.4% for the discrete swaps alone, 79.3% for the field alone). Applying the 105 real bad-pixel masks with median filling then collapsed the ensemble's C/O coverage from 0.901 to 0.479; retraining on the same mask distribution and pooling three such seeds returns a nominal 0.905 C/O and 0.891 overall under the full deployment path, still in simulation (n=1024, same 105 masks), at 0.21 to 0.31 of the prior width. On 105 JWST/G395H spectral products of 13 late-T/Y dwarfs, single marginalized networks bracket the Hood et al. (2024) T8 benchmark C/O where the control excludes it, a consistency check rather than a validation, at 1.6-2.6x wider intervals.

title: Reducing TLS loss in tantalum CPW resonators using titanium sacrificial layers
abstract: We demonstrate a substantial reduction in two-level system loss in tantalum coplanar waveguide resonators fabricated on high-resistivity silicon substrates through the use of an ultrathin titanium sacrificial layer. A 2 Å titanium film, deposited atop pre-sputtered α-tantalum, acts as a solid-state oxygen getter that chemically modifies the native Ta oxide at the metal–air interface. After device fabrication, the titanium layer is removed using buffered oxide etchant, leaving behind a chemically reduced Ta oxide surface. Subsequent high-vacuum annealing further suppresses two-level system loss. Resonators treated with this process exhibit internal quality factors Qi exceeding an average of 1.5 × 106 in the single-photon regime across ten devices—over three times higher than otherwise identical devices lacking the titanium layer. These results highlight the critical role of interfacial oxide chemistry in superconducting loss and reinforce atomic-scale surface engineering as an effective approach to improving coherence in tantalum-based quantum circuits. The method is compatible with existing fabrication workflows applicable to tantalum films, offering a practical route to further extending T1 lifetimes in superconducting qubits.

title: C-DiffSET: Leveraging Latent Diffusion for SAR-to-EO Image Translation with Confidence-Guided Reliable Object Generation
abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery provides robust environmental and temporal coverage (e.g., during clouds, seasons, day-night cycles), yet its noise and unique structural patterns pose interpretation challenges, especially for non-experts. SAR-to-EO (Electro-Optical) image translation (SET) has emerged to make SAR images more perceptually interpretable. However, traditional approaches trained from scratch on limited SAR-EO datasets are prone to overfitting. To address these challenges, we introduce Confidence Diffusion for SAR-to-EO Translation, called C-DiffSET, a framework leveraging pretrained Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) extensively trained on natural images, thus enabling effective adaptation to the EO domain. Remarkably, we find that the pretrained VAE encoder aligns SAR and EO images in the same latent space, even with varying noise levels in SAR inputs. To further improve pixel-wise fidelity for SET, we propose a confidence-guided diffusion (C-Diff) loss that mitigates artifacts from temporal discrepancies, such as appearing or disappearing objects, thereby enhancing structural accuracy. C-DiffSET achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on multiple datasets, significantly outperforming the very recent image-to-image translation methods and SET methods with large margins.

title: A Survey of What to Share in Federated Learning: Perspectives on Model Utility, Privacy Leakage, and Communication Efficiency
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a secure paradigm for collaborative training among clients. Without data centralization, FL allows clients to share local information in a privacy-preserving manner. This approach has gained considerable attention, promoting numerous surveys to summarize the related works. However, the majority of these surveys concentrate on FL methods that share model parameters during the training process, while overlooking the possibility of sharing local information in other forms. In this paper, we present a systematic survey from a new perspective of what to share in FL, with an emphasis on the model utility, privacy leakage, and communication efficiency. First, we present a new taxonomy of FL methods in terms of three sharing methods, which respectively share model, synthetic data, and knowledge. Second, we analyze the vulnerability of different sharing methods to privacy attacks and review the defense mechanisms. Third, we conduct extensive experiments to compare the learning performance and communication overhead of various sharing methods in FL. Besides, we assess the potential privacy leakage through model inversion and membership inference attacks, while comparing the effectiveness of various defense approaches. Finally, we identify future research directions and conclude the survey.

title: From Weights to Words: Representation in Neuroevolution and Explainable AI
abstract: In evolutionary computing, representation is the encoding we choose for a problem. It defines the search space, determines which operations are possible, and embodies the designer's beliefs about what is important. Generally, it is understood that we should design the representation for the algorithm to efficiently solve the problem, which often coincides with the way humans understand the problem as well. However, this is not necessarily the case. Neural networks are conventionally represented as tensors of weights: ideally suited for gradient descent, but poorly suited for both evolutionary optimization and human comprehension. The work in this thesis spans a period when rapid scaling transformed the landscape of AI, solving many problems using general methods and raw compute rather than specialized representations. This thesis asks: if general methods can solve the problem, is there value to a specialized representation? I argue that the primary value of a specialized representation is not task performance, which scaling of general methods has repeatedly delivered, but human understanding -- and that the primary audience of such a representation is ultimately the human, rather than the algorithm. The chapters begin with neuron-level representations, where I present a permutation-invariant encoding for neural networks which preserves more function under crossover than weight-based representation. Next, I consider subnetworks, treating a pruned subnetwork at initialization as a transferable unit. I show that it transfers across initializations, and propose an evolutionary procedure for re-initializing and re-pruning the subnetwork that improves its performance. Third, I present my contributions to OpenELM, an open-source library for evolution using large language models. Here, the representation is a human-understandable object, such as a prompt or code. Finally, I propose explanation-first XAI, inverting the standard pipeline. Explanations come first and explanation quality becomes the primary target of optimization. I evaluate explanations as communication tools by both modeling and testing audience understanding. Rather than designing the representation for task performance and making explainability a secondary consideration, I put explainability at the forefront, and task performance becomes secondary. I believe this is a choice that we will need to make increasingly often, as models continue to scale while human understanding remains fixed.

title: Efficient Construction of Complement-Free and Reverse-Complement-Free Sequences
abstract: Complement-free and reverse-complement-free sequences are cyclic sequences in which the appearance of a length-n substring forbids its complement, or respectively its reverse complement. These constraints arise in DNA computing, where reverse-complementary substrings cause strands to fold into unwanted secondary structures. This thesis presents the first efficient construction for both families over alphabets of arbitrary size. Using a weight-based partition of all strings, we derive upper bounds on their maximum length, then identify rotation-closed k-suffix languages whose necklaces, concatenated in lexicographic order, yield valid sequences using the framework of Sawada, Williams, and Wong (The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 2016). The algorithm runs in O(1)-amortized time per symbol using O(n) space. We prove it is asymptotically optimal, meeting the upper bound exactly for odd n in the complement-free case and producing the longest known reverse-complement-free sequences for every even n > 2 tested.

title: DESIGNING AN AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE INSTRUCTIONAL MODEL FOR LIFE SCIENCE CLASSROOMS: A LEARNING ANALYTICS– BASED ANALYSIS OF PERSONALIZATION, ENGAGEMENT, AND CONCEPTUAL UNDERSTANDING
abstract: Artificial intelligence is starting to reshape the educational practice and become more responsive, data-driven, and learner-focused across a significantly wider scope of instructions.Traditional uniform teaching methods may be ineffective in meeting the needs of the various students in Life Science classrooms where students can be of differing levels of prior knowledge, they can have different learning styles, and conceptual clarity levels.In this paper, we will be discussing the design of an AI-based adaptive instructional model, one that relies on learning analytics to enhance individualization, student interaction, and conceptual comprehension.The paper seeks to explore the way adaptive systems that use AI can assist teachers in modifying content, delivery pace, assessment, and feedback based on student performance and interaction.It is suggested that an analytical framework based on learning analytics will be used to capture the student behavior and identify the gaps in the learning and direct real-time adjustment in the instructional plans of Life Science learning.It is believed that the model will help to enhance learner engagement, maintain their academic interest, and increase the knowledge base about the fundamental concepts in biology by providing customized learning opportunities and support in a reasonable time.It is also aimed at helping educators to make evidence-based pedagogical choices based on data dashboards and predictive insights.The importance of the research has been suggested to address the gap between educational technology and classroom pedagogy which provides the subject specific, scaling and practical model of enhancing teaching effectiveness and student learning outcome in Life Science classrooms.

title: The Target Comes From the Data: What Self-Supervised Learning Actually Learns
abstract: Self-supervised learning is often described as learning from data without labels. This description is useful but incomplete. A self-supervised encoder still depends on a chosen pretext target, representation, corruption rule, architecture, latent dimension, validation split, and audit boundary. This paper evaluates 72 self-supervised encoders on the 307 development vehicles from the complete-case Auto MPG data. Four representations are crossed with masked reconstruction, denoising reconstruction, and contrastive learning, with six parameter settings per family. Five expanding validation years select one encoder per representation-family group, yielding 12 primary models without consulting mpg, origin, or the later population. Across the 12 primary encoders, mean cross-encoder 10-nearest-neighbor Jaccard agreement is 0.350, with a minimum of 0.069. Mean pairwise-distance Spearman is 0.834. Mean input-embedding neighborhood fidelity is 0.590, but the minimum is 0.068. Under 20 deterministic 1% retraining perturbations, mean neighborhood stability is 0.844, while the least stable primary encoder falls to 0.280. The best frozen mpg linear probe reaches temporal R² 0.158, compared with 0.057 for the standardized input baseline. The strongest frozen origin probe reaches macro-F1 0.536. These probes are downstream audits only: mpg and origin do not select, tune, or train the self-supervised encoders. The findings show that a target generated from the data is still a target. Self-supervision can preserve useful information, but it does not define a unique representation by itself. The deposit includes the complete paper and a reproducibility package containing source code, data, machine-readable results for all 72 candidates, 12 selected encoders, frozen embeddings, two 12 × 12 agreement matrices, five generated figures, 20 deterministic perturbation audits per primary encoder, a SHA-256 integrity manifest, and an automated verifier.

title: RICIS-III Formalization of the AGI Target Function: Path-Indexed Objective via SP4 and L1 Identity
abstract: This note formalizes the AGI target function node inside the author-defined RecursiveIndexed Calculus of Identity and Singularity (RICIS-III). title: Core Claim: Design a dynamic graph-based logic formula that dynamically adjusts the logic rules based on input data, enabling more flexible logical operations and handling dynamic data scenarios.
abstract: The development of robust and adaptable logical reasoning systems is crucial across numerous domains, from artificial intelligence to complex decision-making. Existing approaches frequently rely on static, predefined logic rules, limiting their ability to effectively respond to dynamic and evolving data. This research introduces a novel approach leveraging dynamic graphs to address this limitation. Dynamic graphs are characterized by their ability to adapt to changing input data, allowing for more flexible and automated logical operations. This paper presents a design for a dynamic graph-based logic formula, which automatically adjusts logic rules based on input data, thereby enhancing the system's responsiveness to dynamic scenarios. The core of this innovation lies in the implementation of a dynamic graph structure that adapts to the data stream, enabling the formula to intelligently adjust its rules in real-time. The system's design incorporates several key mechanisms to ensure adaptability and efficiency. Specifically, the algorithm incorporates a mechanism for identifying and adapting to data shifts, utilizing a layered approach to dynamically update the graph's structure. This results in a system capable of handling complex, variable-data inputs more effectively than traditional approaches. The paper will detail the architecture of the dynamic graph, explore the algorithm's performance characteristics, and present preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The benefits of this design are highlighted through a discussion of its potential applicability across a range of real-world scenarios, including data analysis, pattern recognition, and automated decision-making.

title: Algorithmic Fairness via Differential Privacy with Personalized Noise Calibration
abstract: Algorithmic fairness has emerged as a critical concern in the deployment of machine learning models, particularly in sensitive domains like hiring, loan applications, and criminal justice. Traditional approaches to fairness often rely on post-processing techniques or modifying the training data, which can introduce biases or compromise model accuracy. This paper proposes a novel framework for achieving algorithmic fairness using differential privacy (DP), coupled with personalized noise calibration. We argue that standard DP, with its assumption of uniform sensitivity, is insufficient for guaranteeing fairness when data distributions across individuals are heterogeneous. Our approach introduces a dynamic noise calibration mechanism that adjusts the privacy budget allocated to each data point based on its sensitivity to protected attributes (e.g., race, gender). This allows us to minimize the overall privacy loss while maximizing fairness, leading to more equitable outcomes. The core claim is that personalized noise calibration is essential for effective DP-based fairness. We detail the algorithm, providing a mathematical formulation of the key components, including sensitivity estimation, noise adjustment, and the overall privacy-fairness trade-off. The framework offers a principled way to balance the competing goals of privacy and fairness in machine learning, paving the way for more trustworthy and responsible AI systems.

title: 基于自适应模型的因果推理与解释
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for causal inference and explanation leveraging adaptive modeling. Traditional causal reasoning methods often rely on static models, limiting the ability to dynamically adjust parameters and improve the accuracy and reliability of inference. Our approach employs an adaptive model, adjusting parameters during the reasoning process to achieve a more robust and accurate causal model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing improved performance in terms of prediction accuracy and explanation quality compared to existing methods. This research contributes to a more nuanced and flexible approach to causal inference, potentially offering significant advancements in various fields requiring robust causal reasoning.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Adaptive Feature Selection
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) offers a paradigm shift in computational power and algorithmic capabilities, potentially revolutionizing various fields, including machine learning. This research explores the application of quantum algorithms to enhance feature selection, a crucial step in many machine learning models. We introduce a novel quantum-enhanced feature selection algorithm, termed "Quantum Feature Selection," which leverages quantum entanglement and superposition to dynamically adjust feature importance during the training process. The core mechanism centers around exploiting these quantum phenomena to guide the selection of the most relevant features, ultimately leading to improved model accuracy and robustness. The algorithm's design aims to surpass existing static feature selection techniques by offering a dynamically adaptive approach. This work presents a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, including theoretical justifications and experimental validation utilizing a diverse dataset. This research is motivated by the potential to address challenges in traditional machine learning, specifically concerning the effective handling of high-dimensional data and the optimization of complex models. Quantum Machine Learning has the potential to provide solutions that are far beyond traditional computational methods.

title: Evaluation Apprehension and Help-Seeking in Learner–AI Interaction: A Randomized 2 × 2 Experiment on Instructor-Access and Tutor-Role Cues
abstract: Artificial tutors can make help continuously available, yet learners may avoid requesting it when the request could reach an evaluative audience. We tested whether two features of that audience—prospective access by the course instructor and an assessing agent role—alter enacted help use while the tutor’s response-generation and scoring pipeline remains constant. In a single-site 2 × 2 randomized experiment, 320 undergraduates were assigned 12 quantitative-reasoning items with the same frozen tutor. Conditions crossed an instructor-linked summary rule (no named summary vs. a named summary eligible for delayed instructor release) with tutor-role framing (practice partner vs. assessing tutor). Across 3,687 observable participant–item opportunities, 1,018 included at least one server-accepted help request; these request-positive opportunities comprised 1,430 accepted request episodes. Logistic generalized estimating equations yielded an equal-item standardized probability of at least one request per opportunity of .359 with no named summary and a practice partner and .217 when both evaluative cues were present. Delayed-release eligibility reduced the request probability by 6.8 percentage points (95% CI [−10.9, −2.7], Holm-adjusted p = .001) and assessing-tutor framing by 7.5 points (95% CI [−11.6, −3.3], Holm-adjusted p < .001). Both cues raised pretask state apprehension, which was inversely associated with requesting; this nonrandomized association is mechanism-consistent, not causal mediation. Access rules and role framing can therefore suppress enacted help use even when the assistance actually delivered is unchanged.

title: Broad-Striped Dasyure Algorithm: A Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm Inspired by the Foraging Behavior of *Sminthopsis brevicauda*
abstract: This paper presents the Broad-Striped Dasyure Algorithm (BSDA), a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of *Sminthopsis brevicauda* (Broad-striped dasyure), a small marsupial renowned for its efficient and adaptive foraging strategies. BSDA leverages the animal's ability to systematically explore and exploit a search space by dividing it into 'strips' and dynamically adjusting its movement based on environmental cues and resource availability. The algorithm incorporates key elements of dasyure behavior, including strip-based exploration, probabilistic movement, and a novel adaptive learning mechanism. We detail the algorithm's design, including the strip generation process, movement probabilities, and the adaptive learning component. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of benchmark problems, showcasing its ability to find optimal or near-optimal solutions with competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic methods. The core of BSDA is the concept of dynamically adjusting exploration and exploitation based on a simulated 'resource density' within each strip. This paper provides a comprehensive description of BSDA, its theoretical foundation, and its practical implementation, offering a potentially valuable addition to the toolbox of metaheuristic optimization techniques.

title: Adaptive Neural Network Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization algorithm for neural networks that dynamically adapts the network's weights based on data distribution. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, rendering them inadequate for data-driven models. This research introduces a framework utilizing neural network's inherent self-adaptation capabilities to iteratively refine weights, leading to enhanced model performance. The core mechanism centers around a continuous, iterative adjustment process that leverages the network's ability to learn complex relationships within the data. We explore a method for determining the optimal weight adjustments through a process of gradient descent, incorporating a novel weighting scheme that mitigates the vanishing gradient problem and promotes faster convergence. The benefits of this adaptive approach are demonstrated through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing superior performance compared to standard optimization techniques.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应矩阵运算 - 动态矩阵的非线性运算
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to matrix operations utilizing quantum entanglement. We propose a method for dynamically modifying matrix operations through entangled states, enabling a non-linear, adaptive process. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the inherent properties of entangled quantum states to induce transformations within the matrix representation. This research explores the potential of this technique for advancing quantum computation, specifically by offering a pathway to circumvent limitations imposed by static matrix representations. The study details the initial setup, the foundational principles, and the initial results of the proposed dynamic matrix operation. The investigation focuses on the mathematical framework underpinning the non-linearity and the potential for practical implementation.

title: Bocage's Rock Rat: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Foraging Behavior of *Oreomys boliviensis*
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, "Bocage's Rock Rat" (BRR), inspired by the foraging strategies of *Oreomys boliviensis*, commonly known as the Bocage's rock rat. These rodents exhibit remarkable spatial memory and efficient resource exploitation in complex, fragmented habitats. BRR leverages these observed behaviors to develop a new optimization approach. The algorithm incorporates elements of path planning, memory retention, and adaptive exploration to navigate solution spaces effectively. Specifically, BRR utilizes a "memory map" to store previously visited solutions, a "pathing" mechanism inspired by the rat's movement patterns, and a "resource allocation" strategy mimicking the rat's selection of food sources. The algorithm is evaluated on several benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its competitiveness and adaptability. The performance analysis reveals that BRR exhibits strong convergence properties and robustness across diverse problem landscapes. The core mathematical formulation of the algorithm is presented, detailing the key parameters and operational rules. This work contributes to the field of metaheuristic optimization by introducing a biologically-inspired approach with demonstrable practical utility.

title: Evaluating the Performance of LYDIA: An AI-Powered Assistant in the Detection of Metastatic Tumors to Optimize Clinical Workflows and Inform Soft Tissue Surgical Decision-Making
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital histopathology has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of metastatic cancer diagnosis. We evaluated LYDIA (LYmph noDe assIstAnt), an AI-based decision-support system, for both standalone diagnostic performance and its impact on histopathologists' workflow, diagnostic accuracy, and resource utilization. LYDIA was evaluated on a blinded dataset of 366 whole-slide images (WSIs) from breast, colorectal, lung, and skin cancers. Standalone performance demonstrated excellent discrimination, achieving ROC-AUC values of 0.995, 0.963, 0.973, and 0.983 for breast, colorectal, lung, and skin cancers, respectively. Clinical utility was further assessed in a multi-reader study involving four experienced histopathologists interpreting 105 WSIs with and without AI assistance. AI-assisted diagnosis significantly reduced time-to-diagnosis across all metastasis sizes, with a maximum 1.59-fold acceleration for micro-metastases, corresponding to a mean time saving of 26.5 s per WSI. LYDIA also improved diagnostic sensitivity from 77.3% to 87.3%. These findings demonstrate that LYDIA can enhance both the efficiency and accuracy of lymph node metastasis detection while reducing diagnostic workload and the need for ancillary testing. Beyond improving routine pathology workflows, the system's rapid inference capabilities and human-expert level performance may support future intraoperative diagnostic applications, enabling timely and automatic or semi-automatic assessment of nodal status to inform surgical decision-making. The resulting reductions in diagnostic time and ancillary testing costs have the potential to improve healthcare resource utilization and patient care, mainly in soft tissue reconstruction and surgical repair decisions.

title: Boundary Screening Bounds the Evidence in Span Masking but Does Not Predict Representation Quality
abstract: Span masking is usually justified informally: contiguous masks are said to force phrase-level rather than token-level inference. We make that argument quantitative and then test it. A boundary-screening theorem shows that the evidence a context carries about a masked set passes entirely through the block boundaries, so it scales with the number of masked blocks rather than the number of masked tokens. The downstream prediction this suggests, registered with decision rules fixed before any run, is refuted. Across a sixteen-fold range of span length at a fixed masking ratio, probe accuracy varies by 0.80 points, a fraction of the 2.0 to 4.3 point changes the same design resolves from auxiliary objectives and from training length. Mask geometry therefore bounds the available evidence without predicting tested representation quality at this scale. Three predictions do hold: the closed form for Gaussian chains matches direct computation to 10-13 nats, a radial conservation law for cosine objectives is recovered in a trained transformer to within 3 percent, and an auxiliary masked-language term improves lexical probes while degrading semantic ones. Encoders are 4.5M parameters trained on 74M tokens, a scale at which the random-initialised baseline is already strong.

title: Academic Paper Classification Method Based on Improved Graph Convolutional Network
authors: YUAN Lining, FENG Wengang, LIU Zhao
abstract: Existing methods used for academic paper classification neglect relational information. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel classification model that integrates a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) with contrastive learning, called a Contrastive Graph Convolutional Network (CGCN). First, two distinct types of homogeneous-heterogeneous relational information are defined based on the content and citations of papers, and they are transformed into self-supervised information to construct contrastive loss. Second, contrastive loss is employed to enhance the feature extraction process of the GCN, such that homogeneous papers are extracted to be close to one another, while heterogeneous papers remain distant. Third, cross-entropy loss and the Softmax function are utilized to complete end-to-end academic paper classification. When tested on three benchmark academic datasets, the CGCN outperforms advanced baselines in the classification task. Its Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 scores are higher than those of the original GCN by 8.29 and 7.91 percentage points, respectively, on the Cora dataset. The CGCN enhances the capacity to represent potential information in papers by employing a contrastive loss based on a homogeneous—heterogeneous relationship, thereby improving the prediction accuracy and generalization. This method provides innovative ideas and methods for academic paper classification.

title: Behavior-triggered self-reflection for zero-shot open-domain UAV target search
abstract: Abstract Open-domain Object Goal Navigation requires a UAV agent to locate arbitrary target objects in previously unseen environments without task-specific training. Existing LLM-based navigation methods often operate in a reactive manner and lack explicit mechanisms for long-term exploration awareness and online self-correction, leading to inefficient behaviors such as revisiting explored regions and getting trapped in local exploration loops. To address these limitations, we propose a closed-loop zero-shot navigation framework that integrates episodic spatial memory and behavior-triggered reflection into the LLM decision process. The memory module summarizes exploration history as a structured language context to improve spatial awareness, while the reflection module detects common navigation failures and provides corrective guidance without additional training or reward signals. Experiments on the UAV-ON benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves navigation success rate and path efficiency over existing zero-shot baselines. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness and complementary roles of episodic memory and behavior-triggered reflection, highlighting the benefit of integrating exploration-aware memory with online self-correction for long-horizon UAV target search.

evidence.title: Behavior-triggered self-reflection for zero-shot open-domain UAV target search
evidence.abstract: Abstract Open-domain Object Goal Navigation requires a UAV agent to locate arbitrary target objects in previously unseen environments without task-specific training. Existing LLM-based navigation methods often operate in a reactive manner and lack explicit mechanisms for long-term exploration awareness and online self-correction, leading to inefficient behaviors such as revisiting explored regions and getting trapped in local exploration loops. To address these limitations, we propose a closed-loop zero-shot navigation framework that integrates episodic spatial memory and behavior-triggered reflection into the LLM decision process. The memory module summarizes exploration history as a structured language context to improve spatial awareness, while the reflection module detects common navigation failures and provides corrective guidance without additional training or reward signals. Experiments on the UAV-ON benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves navigation success rate and path efficiency over existing zero-shot baselines. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness and complementary roles of episodic memory and behavior-triggered reflection, highlighting the benefit of integrating exploration-aware memory with online self-correction for long-horizon UAV target search.

title: Diversity in the impact of heterogeneities on recurrent networks performing a cognitive task
abstract: Artificial recurrent networks are widely used to model the complex dynamics of biological neural circuits performing cognitive tasks. Yet, most studies assume homogeneous units, ignoring functionally important neural heterogeneities. We present a systematic framework to quantify the impact of heterogeneities on recurrent networks performing a cognitive task. We trained a population of networks, differing in hyperparameters, with six graded levels of intrinsic heterogeneities. Our analyses unveiled a surprising diversity in the impact of intrinsic heterogeneities on training, task-execution dynamics, and robustness, despite identical training conditions. First, the dependence of training performance on heterogeneity levels showed pronounced network-to-network variability. Second, task-execution dynamics exhibited marked variability in their dependence on heterogeneities. Finally, post-training perturbations strongly affected robustness, manifesting substantial network-specific variability. This striking diversity in the impact of heterogeneities underscores the need to consider global structure, interactions, and adaptations across multiple heterogeneities to understand collective function in complex neural circuits.

title: Probing Warmth-Mediated Harm in Speech-Enabled LLMs for Mental-Health Conversations
abstract: Audio LLM benchmarks measure understanding and dialogue quality, not whether speech-enabled models respond with relational warmth when a vulnerable user discloses a mental-health concern. We introduce a 7-turn scripted-disclosure probe grounded in WHO mental-health clinical guidelines, with each script run on the same model (Azure OpenAI gpt-realtime) in both audio and text-only conditions, and acoustic-prosody analysis of the generated speech. Across 532 responses we identify two audio-specific patterns transcript-only evaluation would miss: at the elicitation turn the model's voice gets shorter, faster, lower-pitched, and quieter rather than warmer (p < .001 for five of seven acoustic features), and the modality gap on relational acceptance, small in aggregate, concentrates in the highest-stakes self-harm/suicide scripts. A two-rater listener study corroborates that perceived warmth is concentrated at specific turns and on bereavement disclosures. Together these patterns indicate that auditing speech-enabled models in mental-health contexts requires evaluating the combined audio-and-text experience the user encounters, not the transcript in isolation. We release the protocol, scoring pipeline, and scripts as a starting point for evaluating speech-enabled models in mental-health contexts.

title: Integrated Laser Scanning and Image-Based Topology Optimization Techniques for Detection and Quantification of Visible and Subsurface Structural Defects
abstract: Reliable characterization of structural defects requires methods capable of resolving both directly observable surface damage and damage that is not visible from the inspected surface. This study presents two complementary non-contact, vision-based approaches for the detection and quantitative characterization of defects in structural components. The first approach employs high-resolution laser scanning to generate three-dimensional (3D) point clouds of damaged steel specimens. Comparative processing of measured and reference point clouds is used to localize damaged regions, quantify geometric loss, and transfer the measured defect geometry to a finite element representation. The second approach combines full-field surface deformation measurements obtained using three-dimensional digital image correlation (3D-DIC) with finite element model updating and topology optimization. In this inverse framework, measured surface response is used to infer subsurface abnormalities through their influence on the spatial distribution of structural response. Experimental steel-beam specimens containing controlled smooth defects and randomly distributed defects are used to evaluate the approaches. Comparisons with milling-based ground-truth measurements demonstrate that both methods can identify and quantify defect geometry, while providing complementary information for visible and subsurface damage assessment. The combined framework establishes a pathway toward high-fidelity, non-contact structural condition assessment and model updating for components with complex and irregular damage.

title: CaRL-EM: Cost-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Entity Matching with LLMs
abstract: Entity matching (EM) requires fine-grained contextual understanding and domain knowledge. Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can serve as strong matchers across domains, but most methods either make independent pairwise decisions or rely on manually designed composite pipelines, thus lacking flexibility in realistic multi-candidate settings. At the same time, they typically ignore inference cost at scale. We formulate LLM-based EM with candidates as a cost-aware sequential decision problem and propose CaRL-EM, a reinforcement learning controller that manages LLM operations. Given the state of an anchor record, its candidate set, and the cost, CaRL-EM adaptively chooses among different operators (Match/Compare/Select/Decide) and model capacities to maximize a quality-cost objective. The policy interacts with abstract operators, allowing the same controller to be reused with different underlying LLM backends at inference time without retraining. Experiments on 7 benchmarks show that CaRL-EM (i) learns to dynamically plan the usage of inexpensive and expensive operators based on task complexity, (ii) achieves robust zero-shot transfer across diverse datasets and domains, and (iii) consistently achieves a better quality-cost trade-off than strong LLM-based baselines and manually designed pipelines, yielding a lower inference cost at comparable or higher quality.

title: Learned image resizing with efficient training (LRET) facilitates improved performance of large-scale digital histopathology image classification models
abstract: Training large-scale, comprehensive histopathology image classification models using deep learning is limited by two key challenges: the small input dimensions of sub-patch images exclude architectural features that are often critical to distinguish classes, and the memory requirements needed to train comprehensive models across numerous classes results in massively protracted training times. We introduce Learned Resizing with Efficient Training (LRET), a novel approach to training large-scale histopathology classification models that preserves architectural features while enabling efficient use of computational resources. We developed two LRET architectures: one using Google's learned resizing (LRET-GLR) and our novel high-dimensional feature embedding method (LRET-HFE). Both couple resizing modules with efficient training techniques to handle large input patches. We evaluated performance on three datasets with varying complexity across five deep convolutional neural network architectures, comparing against bilinear resizing and direct training without resizing. LRET methods seamlessly integrated with diverse network architectures and adapted to multiple input dimensions. On a 74-class brain tumor dataset, LRET-HFE significantly improved training efficiency while achieving 94.16% accuracy (weighted F1 score: 0.94), representing a 19.2% improvement over bilinear resizing. Visualization of deep learned feature embeddings demonstrated the model captured meaningful representations, effectively separating tumor lineages and distinguishing tumor from normal tissue. LRET methods make training large comprehensive histopathology classification models from scratch computationally feasible by improving training efficiency while maintaining high accuracy. This approach enables training of models that capture a pathologist-level field of view and span the number of tumor classes encountered in clinical practice, facilitating broader applications in computational pathology.

title: Efficient Inference on High-Dimensional Linear Models with Missing Outcomes
abstract: This paper is concerned with inference on the regression function of a high-dimensional linear model when outcomes are missing at random. We propose an estimator that combines a Lasso pilot estimate of the regression function with a bias correction term based on the weighted residuals of the Lasso regression. The weights depend on estimates of the missingness probabilities (propensity scores) and solve a convex optimization program that trades off bias and variance optimally. Provided that the propensity scores can be pointwise consistently estimated at in-sample data points, our proposed estimator for the regression function is asymptotically normal and semiparametrically efficient among all asymptotically linear estimators. Furthermore, the proposed estimator retains its asymptotic properties even if the propensity scores are estimated by modern machine learning techniques. We validate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimator through comparative simulation studies and the real-world problem of inferring the stellar masses of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.

title: Qubits of a Feather, Flawed Together: A Critical Survey Review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared in the context of Physics. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of quantum computing and qubits as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Physics.

title: CloudMig-Ontology: A Domain Ontology for Cloud Migration Decision-Making in Proprietary Software Ecosystems
abstract: Cloud migration has become a strategic imperative for organizations modernizing their legacy systems within Proprietary Software Ecosystems (PSECO). However, selecting an appropriate migration strategy involves complex trade-offs among technical, business, governance, and sustainability factors. This knowledge is often tacit, fragmented across organizational silos, and insufficiently formalized, limiting systematic reuse and decision transparency. To address this gap, this paper presents the CloudMig-Ontology, a domain ontology for formally representing knowledge related to cloud migration decision-making in PSECO. The ontology was developed from a participative case study in a large international organization and integrates concepts related to migration strategies, technical constraints, governance mechanisms , sustainability goals, legacy dependencies, and decision criteria. Development followed the OntoView methodology, with implementation in OWL using Protégé. Validation was performed through competency questions derived from the empirical study and the decision tree artifact proposed in prior research. The results indicate that the ontology can represent and relate the main concepts identified in the domain, providing a structured basis for knowledge reuse, semantic queries, and automated decision-support tools to assist IT managers in migration planning.

title: Cave Bear: A Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm Inspired by Cave Bear Behavior
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm, termed "Cave Bear," inspired by the foraging and navigation strategies observed in cave bears. The algorithm leverages concepts of spatial exploration, resource allocation, and risk assessment, mimicking the bear's behavior in seeking out food sources within a complex and potentially hazardous environment. Cave Bear employs a modified Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) framework, integrating a dynamic territory allocation mechanism and a probabilistic risk avoidance system. The core of the algorithm lies in the concept of "territoriality," where particles represent potential solutions and dynamically adjust their positions based on the perceived quality of neighboring regions and the inherent uncertainty of the search space. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through a series of benchmark functions, demonstrating its ability to converge to optimal or near-optimal solutions efficiently. Key features include a dynamically adjusted inertia weight, a novel territory boundary mechanism, and an adaptive risk aversion parameter. The results suggest that Cave Bear offers a competitive alternative to established metaheuristic algorithms, particularly in challenging optimization landscapes. The algorithm's performance is analyzed and compared against other popular methods like PSO and Genetic Algorithm.

title: Self-Adaptive Chaos Systems Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on adaptive chaos systems, designed to dynamically adjust optimization parameters based on the system's current state. The core mechanism involves the implementation of an adaptive learning algorithm, which continuously refines optimization parameters to achieve improved performance. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, which struggle to adapt to dynamic systems. This self-adaptive approach promises to enhance system performance by providing a more robust and flexible optimization strategy. The research explores the potential benefits of this methodology in various application domains.

title: Title: Adaptive Non-Euclidean Probability Space for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the application of an adaptive non-Euclidean probability space to enhance the performance of machine learning models, particularly in the context of data distribution shift and generalization. Traditional probabilistic models often rely on static probability spaces, limiting their ability to effectively handle data variations. We propose a novel approach that dynamically adjusts the probability space representation based on data characteristics, creating a 'moving probability space' that incorporates the data itself. This mechanism fosters improved robustness and generalization capabilities across diverse datasets. The core of our work lies in the development of a probabilistic metric that continuously evolves to reflect the data's intricacies, ensuring the model adapts to changing conditions. This addresses a critical limitation of existing approaches, offering a pathway towards more robust and adaptable machine learning algorithms.

title: Self-Adaptive Feature Selection and Resampling
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to feature selection and resampling, leveraging a self-adaptive mechanism to dynamically adjust feature selection strategies. The core idea is to implement a feedback loop that continuously evaluates the performance of feature selection and resampling on a dataset, adjusting the parameters to optimize for improved model performance. This contrasts with traditional methods that often rely on static configurations. The implementation details are discussed, and the potential benefits of this approach are highlighted. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the self-adaptive system through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, revealing enhanced performance and robustness.

title: Broad-faced Potoroo Metaheuristic Algorithm (BPMA)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, the Broad-faced Potoroo Metaheuristic Algorithm (BPMA), inspired by the foraging behavior of the broad-faced potoroo ( *Setonix brachyurus*). The algorithm leverages the potoroo's unique ability to efficiently navigate complex terrains and locate food sources, translating these characteristics into a robust optimization strategy. BPMA incorporates elements of particle swarm optimization (PSO) and simulated annealing (SA) with modifications designed to enhance exploration and exploitation capabilities. Specifically, the algorithm utilizes a "territory" concept, mimicking the potoroo's established foraging areas, and a dynamic adaptation of the inertia weight and cognitive/social parameters based on simulated food availability. The performance of BPMA is evaluated on several benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and competitive results against established metaheuristic algorithms. The key contributions of this work include the formulation of a novel algorithm design based on animal behavior and its successful application to various optimization tasks. evidence.title: Broad-faced Potoroo Metaheuristic Algorithm (BPMA)
evidence.abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, the Broad-faced Potoroo Metaheuristic Algorithm (BPMA), inspired by the foraging behavior of the broad-faced potoroo ( *Setonix brachyurus*). The algorithm leverages the potoroo's unique ability to efficiently navigate complex terrains and locate food sources, translating these characteristics into a robust optimization strategy. BPMA incorporates elements of particle swarm optimization (PSO) and simulated annealing (SA) with modifications designed to enhance exploration and exploitation capabilities. Specifically, the algorithm utilizes a "territory" concept, mimicking the potoroo's established foraging areas, and a dynamic adaptation of the inertia weight and cognitive/social parameters based on simulated food availability. The performance of BPMA is evaluated on several benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and competitive results against established metaheuristic algorithms. The key contributions of this work include the formulation of a novel algorithm design based on animal behavior and its successful application to various optimization tasks. The algorithm's core mechanisms and their theoretical underpinnings are detailed, providing a clear and understandable framework for further research and development.

title: Quantum Annealing for Constraint Satisfaction Problems with Temporal Constraints
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum annealing to Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) that incorporate temporal constraints. Traditional quantum annealing approaches often falter when dealing with these more complex scenarios. We propose an adaptive strategy that reformulates the CSP into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem, strategically incorporating operators designed to explicitly represent and enforce temporal dependencies. Our approach aims to enhance the algorithm's ability to navigate problems where solutions are not just determined by logical constraints but also by their timing. The core of our methodology lies in translating the temporal logic directly into the quantum annealing framework, allowing for a more nuanced and effective exploration of the solution space. We demonstrate the potential of this method through a theoretical analysis and formulation, focusing on the key elements required for successful implementation within a quantum annealing system. This work represents a direct response to the limitations of current quantum annealing techniques and offers a novel pathway for tackling temporally constrained CSPs.

title: Context-Aware Graph Embeddings for Social Network Analysis
abstract: Traditional graph embeddings, such as Node2Vec and Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), often represent social networks as static snapshots, neglecting the dynamic and context-dependent nature of relationships. This research proposes a novel approach to graph embedding that incorporates contextual information, leading to more accurate and nuanced representations of social networks. Our method dynamically updates embedding vectors based on factors like user activity, location, and time. We introduce a framework that allows for capturing the evolving relationships within a network. The core idea is to move beyond static representations and create embeddings that reflect the real-time context of social interactions. The resulting embeddings are evaluated through simulations and theoretical analysis, demonstrating significant improvements in capturing network dynamics compared to traditional methods. The key contributions include the development of a context-aware graph embedding algorithm and a theoretical framework for understanding its impact on network representation. The algorithm utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to process contextual information and update the graph embeddings. We also explore different weighting strategies for contextual features to optimize the embedding quality.

title: Explainable AI for Conditional Stroke Probability Estimation: A Hybrid Bayesian Network Approach
abstract: Accurate stroke prediction is vital for early intervention, yet most high-performing AI/ML models remain “black boxes” with little intrinsic interpretability. Bayesian net-works (BNs) are probabilistic graphical models that balance predictive performance with interpretable, auditable reasoning. We assessed whether optimizing data preprocessing could enhance BNs diagnostic performance on a highly imbalanced stroke dataset. Using a 2×2×2 factorial design, we compared eight configurations varying three choices: dis-cretized versus continuous (conditional Gaussian) topology, median versus multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), and no balancing versus synthetic over-sampling (SMOTE). Preserving continuous variables significantly improved discrimina-tion over discretization (AUC 0.812 vs 0.718; p = 0.011), an advantage that persisted across 30 stratified resamples (paired p < 0.001); the hybrid BN matched XGBoost (0.822) and logistic regression (0.819). MICE gave no advantage over median substitution (p = 0.708), and SMOTE did not improve performance while tripling the Brier score, indicating posterior miscalibration. The optimal BN remained interpretable and could simulate illustrative absolute risk reductions (e.g., 43.18% to 31.55% under modelled glycemic control). Continuous BNs offer an interpretable, well-calibrated, and robust framework for clinical decision support, warranting prospective validation in real-world settings.

title: Wikidata: The Final Frontier for Ontology?
abstract: The Wikidata knowledge graph describes 121 million entities connected by 13 thousand different types of relations. It is edited by over 40 thousand active editors, and supports more than 350 natural languages. Relations are viewed as claims: Wikidata presents the relation shape(Earth,geoid) alongside shape(Earth,disk). Claims can be annotated with time, references, provenance and confidence, to name a handful of examples. Some claims one can find in Wikidata are ontological, for example that “fictional human” is a subclass of “imaginary human”, which is a subclass of “imaginary character”, which is a subclass of “non-existent entity”, which is a subclass of “entity”, which is an instance of “variable-order class”, which is an instance of itself. This talk will introduce Wikidata as a unique challenge, and potentially a final frontier, for ontology. We will give an overview of the knowledge graph, its applications, its potential, and its ontological bricolage. We motivate the opportunities for work on ontological modelling that is understandable for (and serves to guide) its thousands of non-expert editors, enables reasoning at massive scale, and makes the lives of the ever-growing Wikidata community easier.

title: Efficient Three-Class Sentiment Classification of IMDb Reviews Using LoRA-Based Fine-Tuning on Pseudo-labeled Data
abstract: Sentiment analysis has become an important task in natural language processing for understanding public opinions expressed in online reviews. However, most publicly available IMDb datasets are limited to binary sentiment labels, which restricts the ability of sentiment analysis systems to capture neutral opinions. This study proposes an efficient sentiment analysis framework that transforms the binary IMDb dataset into a three-class sentiment classification problem consisting of positive, neutral, and negative sentiments. The proposed approach integrates pseudolabeling with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) using the Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) technique on the Longformer architecture. Experimental results show that the model achieves an accuracy of 77.06%, a weighted F1-score of 72.17%, and a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.6232. The results demonstrate that LoRA-based fine-tuning can significantly reduce computational requirements while maintaining competitive performance in sentiment classification tasks. These findings indicate that the proposed framework provides a practical and computationally efficient solution for large-scale sentiment analysis, particularly for environments with limited computational resources.

title: Design and Initial Evaluation of a RAG-Based Expert Chatbot for User Support in Non-Destructive Testing
abstract: Inspection personnel need exact parameters and safety limits from proprietary documentation that may be unsuitable for hosted processing. We present a local Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot for Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) manuals and a controlled benchmark comprising three synthetic manuals, 60 curated questions, and 267 predefined required facts. Answers were scored using Key Fact Coverage (KFC), the proportion of facts detected by a deterministic matcher. A full-factorial sweep of 32 configurations reached a maximum KFC of 0.789. Document access yielded larger gains than the within-pipeline variations tested: six closed-book systems scored 0.248 to 0.339, and all four prespecified comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (adjusted p ≤ 0.0028). Synthetic specifications reduced the likelihood of answer memorization. The chunking configuration produced the clearest within-pipeline difference: the 1,000-token condition outperformed the 5,000-token condition in all 16 matched pairs (+0.161, p < 0.001). Hybrid retrieval improved KFC by 0.11 to 0.12, mainly for table questions. This is an initial controlled benchmark, not evidence of industrial robustness.

title: Far-field earthquake information from single-station waveforms: The 2026 MW6.8 Kumamoto earthquake
abstract: On July 28, 2026, at 15:27:15.512 Beijing Time (07:27:15.512 UTC), an MW6.8 earthquake occurred in the Kumamoto region of Japan. This study reviewed one operational run of a prototype system using three-component waveforms from Global Seismographic Network station IU.MAJO. The deployed DiTing model component processed the continuous waveform stream, identified the P-wave onset, produced preliminary event parameters, and recorded the completion of the server-side MQTT push. IU.MAJO is located approximately 808.7 km from the USGS catalog epicenter, with a forward azimuth of 55.9° from the epicenter to the station. The system P-wave first-arrival pick at 07:29:03.595 UTC occurred 108.1 s after the cataloged origin time and 1.9 s after the theoretical P-wave first arrival predicted by iasp91; This difference arises from the theoretical arrival rather than an error relative to the manual pick. The estimated system magnitude was M6.86, a numerical difference of 0.06 from the MW6.8 provided by the USGS. The server-side MQTT push was completed 57.9 s after the P-wave pick and 166.0 s after the catalog origin time. The estimated origin time was 80.1 s later than the observed, and the reported location was approximately 982.1 km from the catalog epicenter, demonstrating substantial limitations in the preliminary single-station time and location estimates. However, the results only document one run for a specific event, station, and data condition. They do not constitute a statistical validation of the model performance or conventional near-source public earthquake early warning systems.

title: Samodejna priprava prometnih poročil za obveščanje javnosti prek radijskih postaj
abstract: V prispevku predstavljamo razvoj sistema za samodejno generiranje prometnih poročil za radijsko poročanje z uporabo velikih jezikovnih modelov. Sistem temelji na podatkih nacionalnega prometnega portala NAP, iz katerega redno pridobiva podatke o prometnih dogodkih in delih na cesti. Pridobljeni podatki se shranjujejo, normalizirajo in pripravijo za nadaljnjo klasifikacijo ter generiranje besedil. Poseben poudarek namenjamo primerjavi različnih pristopov k uporabi jezikovnih modelov, in sicer tako modelov v oblaku kot lokalno naučenih oziroma prilagojenih modelov. Primerjavo izvajamo za naloge klasifikacije prometnih dogodkov in generiranja prometnih poročil, pri čemer upoštevamo kakovost izhodov, hitrost odziva, stroške uporabe, robustnost in primernost za slovenski jezik. Za generiranje rednih prometnih poročil uporabljamo dvostopenjski pristop, pri katerem se prometni zapisi najprej pretvorijo v strukturirane semantične fragmente, nato pa v končno slovensko besedilo, primerno za radijsko branje. Prispevek obravnava podatkovni cevovod, obdelavo vhodnih podatkov, primerjavo modelov in vlogo človeka pri končni uredniški presoji.

title: Identificación de parámetros en cavidades cuánticas abiertas
abstract: Characterizing environmental noise in open quantum systems is a key challenge in quantum technologies. In this work, this problem is addressed through a frequency-domain framework based on Volterra series, which enables the description of the dynamics by means of generalized frequency response functions (GFRFs). We show that two-tone excitation generates spectral mixing components containing information about both the system parameters and the environmental noise, enabling their simultaneous estimation even in the presence of experimental noise. Our results establish nonlinear spectral mixing as an effective tool for inferring properties of both the system and the environment from frequency-domain measurements.

title: Iterative verification-driven collaboration of fine-tuned models and large language models for named entity recognition
abstract: As data becomes a pivotal factor of production in the digital economy, the process of data factorization relies heavily on precise Named Entity Recognition (NER) to extract key entities from unstructured text, thereby facilitating data governance and intelligent applications. While fine-tuned models (Small Language Models, SLMs) are computationally efficient, they often struggle with Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) entities due to data limitations. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) possess extensive knowledge bases but suffer from poor domain adaptability and high computational costs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a collaborative framework between fine-tuned models and LLMs. In this framework, the fine-tuned model performs initial annotation, followed by an uncertainty estimation method to filter low-confidence entity candidates. These candidates are then forwarded to the LLM for review and correction. The LLM employs a self-feedback mechanism to iteratively verify entities until convergence. Furthermore, we introduce a unified code-style schema to guide LLM outputs, ensuring structured results and task-specific focus. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances both accuracy and generalization in NER tasks while reducing the computational overhead of LLMs. This research provides technical support for the precise extraction of data elements and promotes intelligent, green data processing.

title: WSI-Babel-Shark: A modular pipeline for robust metadata extraction from heterogeneous whole-slide image labels in digital pathology
abstract: Introduction Automated extraction of slide metadata remains a major bottleneck in digital pathology, especially in settings where barcode identifiers are missing, damaged, or inconsistent. Manual transcription of case, block, and stain information is error-prone and does not scale. Building on our previous whole-slide image (WSI)-Babel-Fish framework, we developed WSI-Babel-Shark, a more extensible pipeline for reliable metadata extraction across heterogeneous slide-label layouts. Materials and methods WSI-Babel-Shark integrates data matrix code decoding, region of interest (ROI)-based optical character recognition (OCR), and rule-based metadata parsing within a modular Python and Docker architecture. To handle diverse institutional label formats, the system incorporates a deep learning-based label layout classifier using a ResNet-18 backbone, fused with handcrafted descriptors and prototype-based open-set recognition to categorize labels into 10 predefined layout groups. A graphical interface supports ROI annotation, dataset management, and configuration editing. Performance was evaluated on 270 WSIs (.svs and .ndpi formats) and cross-validated using 110 slides from the previously published WSI-Babel-Fish dataset to assess backward compatibility. Results The label layout classifier achieved an overall accuracy of 97.4%, with macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.98 while reliably rejecting previously unseen layouts. End-to-end pipeline evaluation achieved complete SlideID reconstruction for 258 of 267 evaluable WSIs (96.6%). Independent comparison of OCR-derived metadata with the corresponding Data Matrix-decoded metadata on 236 slides demonstrated complete metadata concordance for 230 slides (97.5%), whereas field-level concordance ranged from 98.3% to 100.0% across all evaluated metadata fields. Cross-dataset analysis confirmed full compatibility with WSI-Babel-Fish label structures. Conclusion WSI-Babel-Shark advances automated metadata extraction from WSIs by introducing a label-layout classification framework validated on heterogeneous label layouts and incorporating open-set recognition, together with standardized ROI annotation and a fully containerized implementation. The framework ensures reproducible linkage between digitized slides and lab information, is designed to facilitate interoperability with lab information systems, and provides a scalable foundation for large-scale digital pathology workflows. The complete implementation is openly available at: https://github.com/cpheidelberg/WSI-Babel-Shark .
